title: TRDP: switch the dissector to the TCNOPEN-community origined version
description:
The current dissector is renamed trdp-eke, as proposed in #19640 and replaced by the so far out-of-tree-plugin "TRDP SPY". Most notable change is the support for payload definitions based on XML-files as defined in the protocols standard IEC 61375-2-3. The dissector includes a base set of standardized data-sets. It can be extended by loading custom XML files through the dissector properties. There are further tweaks possible through the settings. Currently, the dissector does not support conversations and neither deep-dives into illegal property values or safety related protocol faults.

Marked as draft, as this is my first merge request.

Issue that triggered this request: #19640 

Previous home / development history of the plugin: https://github.com/t12z/tcnopen

I am not an official member of https://www.tcnopen.eu/, yet in active contact with project leads.

clang fails (only compiled by gcc locally) due to recursion. Recursion of data-structures in general is a basic feature of TRDP - yet not of the same data-structures - which would make it endless.

This is more than a one-line fix and will need some time and thought.

That's an warning from clang-tidy we turn on, but it can be disabled with a line like:

`// NOLINTNEXTLINE(misc-no-recursion)`

E.g., https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-tls-utils.c#L11757

Do be careful when disabling it that you can demonstrate that, e.g., the offset into the packet data always advances and will not overflow and wrap around or otherwise go back to a previous value or stay the same due to fuzzed or otherwise buggy data. We have it in there to prevent infinite loops (and at least make developers think hard about whether there can be an infinite loop.)

Thanks John for the helping hints.

I thought about finding a non-recursive approach, but it would have been worse. There is a word on this in https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/doc/README.developer?ref_type=heads#L720 , which I missed.

In the one case I added `increment_dissection_depth()` as guard, in the actually "vulnerable" case, previously I only guarded against direct recursion, never cyclic. That has been updated and I also introduced a maximum recursion limit.

After further discussion with John below I think I understood the pros and cons of the initial approach, which lead to rewriting that part to delayed run-time-loading of the xml-file, like wimax / diameter / tpncp do it.
The name of this script is very generic. Can it be renamed to clearly show the use case?

technically, it is a generic file to header tool.

Now, from the perspective of the other comment, on moving the resource and seeing how wimaxasncp and diameter plugins leave their XMLs outside for runtime loading, would this be the preferred choice instead of embedding as a blob? I guess there are pros and cons to either approach, what would be preferred?

The disadvantage of this script is that it looks like it would require recompilation if people supplied their own XML files. That seems less appropriate for the official Wireshark distribution.

The con is that it is faster to turn it into a C header. Reading from text files is slow, so the Diameter and other plugins do some tricks to avoid loading their XML until needed (e.g., when the protocol is encountered.)

Hej John,
thanks for the valuable feedback! However, there is no actual header-code-conversion. The idea was only in saving the extra file access and load at wireshark-start. The XML-Parsing is rerun at each loading of the dissector. I have not come up with any to-C-struct-conversion. 

Currently, one can run-time-load multiple additional xml-files, as long as they don't conflict. This is typically needed, since each component in a train control may supply their own xml definitions and it'd be painful to merge those.

The included xml is the first and initial to be loaded. I added a dissector property not to load the initial definitions, for if they conflict with some custom-non-standard-proprietary defs. So this would not become a blocker in the future.

Alternatively, what I could think of right now, is to delay the xml loading until a first call to the dissector, so there is less impact on users not involved with TRDP.

I'm a little confused because the Python script says it generates C code in the comments. We have two general approaches:

1. Code or scripts in tools/ (which can be scripts in Python, Perl, etc.) that generate C code. This is for dissectors based on external definitions like IDL or ASN.1, or for external data like ID to manufacturer strings in protocols like Bluetooth. This is best for when there's some kind of central repository for the external data and all users interested in that protocol will want to use the same updates.
2. Dissectors that place data in resources/protocols/{protoname}. This textual data is read by dissectors using C code (whether flex-based parsers or file reading libraries like libxml2), possibly delayed until the protocol is actually seen (or the user requests output on all protocols), as done by RADIUS, Diameter, WiMAXSNCP, etc. because even with C code reading text based configuration files can add a noticeable amount to the startup time. These could possibly be affected by protocol preferences, including examining additional user-specified directories.

I don't believe that we have anything where we run Python scripts at run-time to parse configuration files. I'd prefer not to do so. Is that what would happen?

Sorry for the confusion.
The python script only includes the xml-file as compressed text-blob in a const-variable, so only generates a c-file with a byte-array, that is then parsed at run-time.
So approach (2) would be the right way to go, which I wasn't correctly aware of.

I will prepare an updated merge in the next days, that moves the xml to resources/protocols/{protoname}, and loads that original xml-file at run-time, however delayed until actual use. (and all without the python script)

Thanks for the clarification, much appreciated!
